pos: n. (one that devours or consumes; that which eats up or destroys)
etymology: Agent noun from devour, from Old French devorer, from Latin devorare, to swallow down whole, de- + vorare, to swallow.
biblical_def:
And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts.

Malachi sets this promise directly after the LORD's challenge to a people who have robbed Him in tithes and offerings, bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, and prove me now herewith. The devourer is the LORD's own name for whatever consumes a harvest before it can be gathered, locusts, blight, untimely drop, the ordinary agricultural disasters of an ancient economy, here identified as something the LORD Himself rebukes on behalf of an obedient, tithing people. The promise is covenantal, not magical: it follows obedience, prove me now herewith, rather than preceding or guaranteeing it, and it is addressed to a specific historical people under a specific covenant arrangement with specific agricultural stakes. Scripture elsewhere names Satan himself a devourer of a different kind, your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour, which should caution against collapsing Malachi's agricultural promise into a universal financial guarantee; the devourer rebuked in Malachi 3 is a particular mercy to a particular covenant people, not a transferable formula for prosperity in every age and economy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DEVOUR: one that devours; that which consumes, wastes, or destroys utterly.
webster_full: DEVOUR, v.t. To eat up with greediness; to consume or destroy rapidly.
DEVOURER, n. One or that which devours; a consumer or destroyer.
Malachi 3: the LORD will rebuke the devourer for the sake of an obedient, tithing people.
Follows directly upon the LORD's challenge to bring the whole tithe into the storehouse.
A covenantal promise tied to obedience, not an unconditional guarantee.
scriptures: Mal 3:11
And I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast her fruit before the time in the field, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel strips the devourer's rebuke from its covenant obedience and markets it as an unconditional return on tithing.
corruption_paragraphs: Prosperity teaching regularly isolates Malachi 3:11 from its context, bring ye all the tithes, and preaches it as a financial transaction: give, and the devourer of debt or lack is automatically rebuked, with giving treated as an investment rather than worship offered to a covenant LORD.

Malachi's own grammar resists this: the rebuke follows a specific call to obedience within a specific covenant, prove me now herewith, and is addressed to a people already under judgment for robbing God, not a formula detached from repentance and offered as a guaranteed exchange. A gospel that promises the devourer rebuked for every giver regardless of the heart's condition has turned a mercy to the obedient into a transaction for the presumptuous.
roots_summary: From Latin devorare, to swallow down, de- intensifying vorare, to swallow, the devourer names whatever consumes a thing whole before its purpose is fulfilled.
roots_lines: Vorare, Latin for to swallow, is intensified by de- into devorare.
Devour names consuming something rapidly and wholly.
Malachi 3 applies devourer to whatever destroys a harvest before its season.
The LORD's rebuke of it follows a specific call to obedient tithing.
Peter elsewhere names Satan a devourer of a different, spiritual kind.
usage: I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes — a covenantal promise, not a formula
follows directly on the call to bring the whole tithe into the storehouse
distinct from Peter's devourer, the adversary who seeks whom he may devour

etymology: From Old French desconfiture, from desconfire, to defeat utterly, from Latin dis- + conficere, to finish or complete; the word names a defeat so total it finishes an army, not merely a setback.
biblical_def:
And Saul and all the people that were with him assembled themselves, and they came to the battle: and, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture.

This discomfiture follows directly on Jonathan's lone, faith-driven assault on the Philistine garrison at Michmash, an act of trust his own father Saul knew nothing about until the chaos was already spreading. The LORD sends an earthquake and panic through the Philistine camp so thorough that every man's sword was against his fellow, the enemy army destroying itself in its own confusion before Israel's forces even arrive in force. Discomfiture names exactly this, not merely losing a battle but losing all ability to fight coherently at all, a rout generated from within rather than inflicted from without. The chapter's quiet theology is that this very great discomfiture began with one young man's small, unauthorized act of faith, Jonathan's confidence that the LORD is not restrained to save by many or by few, while Saul, the anointed king, was counting soldiers under a pomegranate tree. The LORD's power to turn an enemy's own army against itself did not wait for royal permission; it followed Jonathan's faith and left Saul merely assembling to receive a victory he had done nothing to secure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISCOMFIT: the act of defeating or routing utterly; a state of total confusion in defeat.
webster_full: DISCOMFIT, v.t. To rout; to defeat and throw into confusion.
DISCOMFITURE, n. Utter defeat; total rout and confusion.
1 Samuel 14: a very great discomfiture seizes the Philistine camp at Michmash.
Follows directly from Jonathan's lone act of faith against the garrison.
A rout generated from within the enemy's own panic, not by Israel's numbers.
scriptures: And Saul and all the people that were with him assembled themselves, and they came to the battle: and, behold, every man's sword was against his fellow, and there was a very great discomfiture.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that faith acts before permission arrives, and the LORD is not bound by numbers.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Discomfiture has simply become an archaic word for embarrassment in common speech, far milder than its biblical sense of total military rout.

The narrative behind it still rebukes a church that waits for consensus or official sanction before acting in faith. Jonathan's small act, taken without his father's knowledge, produced a discomfiture no royal strategy had planned for, a reminder that the LORD is not restrained to save by many or by few, and often moves ahead of the very leaders counting soldiers under a tree.
roots_summary: From Latin conficere, to finish or complete, negated by dis-, discomfiture names a finishing turned to ruin: an army's total, self-inflicted undoing.
roots_lines: Conficere, Latin for to finish or complete, is negated by dis- into disconfire.
Discomfit names a rout; discomfiture, the resulting state of total confusion.
1 Samuel 14 applies it to the Philistine camp's self-inflicted panic at Michmash.
The rout follows Jonathan's lone act of faith, unknown to Saul.
Illustrates that the LORD saves by many or by few without distinction.
usage: there was a very great discomfiture — a rout the Philistines inflicted on themselves
follows Jonathan's unauthorized act of faith at the garrison
the LORD is not restrained to save by many or by few

pos: v.t. (to mar the figure or appearance of; to deform)
etymology: From Old French desfigurer, from Latin dis- + figurare, to shape or form; to unmake the very shape a thing was given.
biblical_def:
Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast.

Jesus is correcting a specific abuse of a genuine spiritual discipline: the hypocrites He names did not merely look sorrowful while fasting, they disfigure their faces, deliberately marring their own appearance, likely through unwashed grime or exaggerated gloom, so that the fast could be seen and credited by onlookers. The sin is not fasting, which Jesus assumes His disciples will continue to do, when thou fastest, but performing fasting for an audience rather than before the Father who seeth in secret. Disfigure makes vivid what hypocrisy always does to the self: it does not merely misrepresent the heart to others, it actively mars the very face God gave, bending a man's own appearance into a billboard for his own supposed piety. Jesus's remedy is strikingly ordinary rather than ascetic, anoint thine head, and wash thy face, that thou appear not unto men to fast, restoring the face to its natural use rather than replacing one performance with another. The passage sits between Christ's teaching on secret almsgiving and secret prayer, forming a triptych of disciplines whose value Jesus roots entirely in their being unseen by men and seen only by the Father, who shall reward thee openly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from DISFIGURE: to mar or deform the figure or form; to make less complete, perfect, or beautiful in appearance.
webster_full: FIGURE, n. The form or shape of a thing; external appearance.
DISFIGURE, v.t. To mar the figure; to deform; to make unsightly.
Matthew 6: the hypocrites disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast.
Sits between Christ's teaching on secret almsgiving and secret prayer.
The remedy Christ gives is ordinary grooming, not a counter-performance.
scriptures: Mat 6:16
Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.
corruption_summary: Public religious performance has migrated from the exaggerated fasting face to the curated spiritual post, but the hypocrisy Jesus names is identical.
corruption_paragraphs: The disfigured face of Matthew 6 has a direct modern heir in the performed piety of social media, the visibly humble caption, the photographed act of charity, the public display engineered to be seen and credited by an audience rather than offered to the Father who seeth in secret.

Jesus's warning applies without modification: they have their reward already, whatever human approval the performance earns, and no further reward is promised from heaven for a piety that was staged for men from the start. The remedy is still the same ordinary unglamorous obscurity, wash thy face, that the Father who sees in secret may be the only audience a true discipline ever needed.
roots_summary: From Latin figurare, to shape or form, negated by dis-, the word names an unmaking of a given shape, applied by Christ to a face marred for an audience's benefit.
roots_lines: Figurare, Latin for to shape, is negated by dis- into disfigurare.

Matthew 6 applies it to hypocrites who mar their own faces to be seen fasting.

pos: v.t. (to cut off from an inheritance; to deprive of a right to inherit)
etymology: From Old French desheriter, from Latin dis- + heres, heir; to unmake a man's standing as heir.
biblical_def:
I will smite them with the pestilence, and disinherit them, and will make of thee a greater nation and mightier than they.

The LORD speaks this to Moses after the ten spies' report has provoked the whole congregation to despair and open rebellion, a generation that has just finished saying let us make a captain, and let us return into Egypt rather than trust the LORD for the land He promised. Disinherit names the LORD's proposed judgment in its starkest form, not merely delay or discipline but the complete severing of this generation's claim to the inheritance their fathers were promised, replacing them with a nation built from Moses alone. What makes the passage theologically weighty is what happens next: Moses intercedes, pardon, I beseech thee, the iniquity of this people, and the LORD relents from this particular form of judgment, choosing instead the forty years of wilderness wandering that disinherits the adults without disinheriting the nation itself, since their children would still enter the land. Disinherit therefore marks the outer edge of covenant judgment that intercession turned aside, not evidence that the LORD's threats are idle, but evidence of exactly how costly, and how real, Moses's intercession was. The inheritance promised to Abraham's seed survived that generation's unbelief only because someone stood in the gap between the threat and its execution.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HEIR, negated by DIS-: to cut off from hereditary right; to deprive of an inheritance already due.
webster_full: HEIR, n. One who inherits, or is entitled to inherit, an estate.
DISINHERIT, v.t. To cut off from an inheritance; to deprive of a right to inherit.
Numbers 14: the LORD proposes to disinherit the unbelieving generation entirely.
Moses intercedes, and the judgment is turned to wilderness wandering instead.
Marks the outer edge of a judgment that intercession turned aside.
scriptures: I will smite them with the pestilence, and disinherit them, and will make of thee a greater nation and mightier than they.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is the weight and cost of real intercession before a real threat.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Disinherit remains chiefly a legal term today, its biblical sense of covenant severance largely forgotten outside the text itself.

The narrative behind it is worth recovering against any flattened doctrine of prayer that treats intercession as merely informing God of a preference rather than genuinely standing in the gap. The LORD's proposal to disinherit this generation was real; Moses's intercession, and the LORD's relenting in response to it, were equally real. Scripture will not let either half be softened into the other.

pos: v., past tense/adj. (caught in a snare; entrapped)
etymology: From en-, a causative prefix, + snare, from Old Norse snara, a noose or trap; to put something into a snare, to make it a thing caught.
biblical_def:
That the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared.

Elihu's speech to Job is building toward a broader defense of the LORD's justice in governing the world, and this clause names one specific mercy within that governance: the LORD acts, sometimes through sudden and seemingly harsh providence, so that the hypocrite reign not, precisely so that an ungodly ruler's deception does not leave an entire people ensnared under his influence. The verse assumes what Scripture states elsewhere without apology, that a nation's spiritual condition is deeply entangled with its rulers, so that a hypocrite on the throne is not a private failing but a public snare set for everyone under his authority. Ensnared pictures the people here as prey rather than merely as the governed, caught unawares in a trap they did not set and may not even see, which is exactly the danger a hypocritical ruler poses: his deception does not announce itself as deception. Elihu's larger point to Job is that the LORD's providence, even when it looks unexplained or severe from the ground, is frequently aimed at preventing exactly this kind of corporate ensnarement, removing a false shepherd before an entire flock is caught in his net.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from SNARE: caught in a snare; entrapped, especially by deceit or an unseen danger.
webster_full: SNARE, n. A noose for catching game; any device for entrapping.
ENSNARE, v.t. To catch in a snare; to entrap by deceit or hidden danger.
Job 34: Elihu names the LORD's purpose that the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared.
Pictures a people as prey caught unawares by a deceiving ruler's influence.
Frames providence, even when severe, as often aimed at preventing such corporate entrapment.
scriptures: That the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that a nation's leadership is never a purely private matter for those it governs.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ensnared remains in common use with its original sense intact, caught in a trap, largely unaltered by modern reinterpretation.

The theology behind Elihu's clause still presses a question a privatized faith would rather avoid: Scripture refuses to treat who governs as a matter indifferent to the governed's spiritual safety. A hypocrite's rise is not merely his own sin; it is, Elihu says, a snare set for an entire people, which is precisely why the LORD's providence is so often concerned with exactly who does, and does not, reign.
roots_summary: From Old Norse snara, a noose, through the causative en-, ensnared names being made the catch of a trap, often one set by deceit rather than force.

pos: adv. (in a wretched manner; with severity or ruin)
etymology: From miserable, from Latin miserabilis, pitiable, from miser, wretched; the adverb marks not just destruction but destruction of a wretched, pitiable kind.
biblical_def:
They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons.

This is the Pharisees' and chief priests' own verdict, pronounced on themselves, after Jesus tells the parable of the vineyard owner whose tenants beat his servants and finally kill his son rather than render him his fruit. Jesus asks them directly what the owner will do, and their answer, he will miserably destroy those wicked men, lands as self-condemnation before they fully realize whom the parable describes; Matthew notes immediately after that they perceived that he spake of them. Miserably intensifies destroy into something beyond ordinary judgment, a ruin fitting the wretchedness of the crime, tenants who had every privilege of the vineyard and repaid it by murdering the owner's own son. The parable's final line supplies the New Testament's own reading of the whole history of Israel's rejected prophets and, climactically, her rejected Messiah: the kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof. The leaders' own mouths pronounce the sentence their own unbelief will shortly bring upon themselves, a pattern Scripture repeats often enough to be its own kind of warning, that unbelief frequently convicts itself before judgment ever needs to be announced from outside.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from MISERABLE: in a wretched, pitiable manner; with severity fitting a wretched cause.
webster_full: MISERABLE, a. Very unhappy; wretched; deserving pity or contempt.
MISERABLY, adv. In a wretched manner; with ruin fitting the cause.
Matthew 21: the vineyard owner will miserably destroy the wicked husbandmen.
Spoken by the chief priests and Pharisees as their own verdict on the parable.
They perceived that he spake of them only after pronouncing the sentence themselves.
scriptures: They say unto him, He will miserably destroy those wicked men, and will let out his vineyard unto other husbandmen, which shall render him the fruits in their seasons.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is how plainly unbelief can convict itself before judgment is announced.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Miserably remains in ordinary use as an intensifier, miserably failed, with little trace left of its sharper biblical weight.

The parable behind it remains a sober warning for any religious establishment confident in its own privileges: the chief priests condemned themselves with their own answer before they understood the question was about them. A church that enjoys every advantage of the vineyard and still refuses to render its fruit to the owner stands exactly where they stood, one perceptive question away from pronouncing its own sentence.

pos: v.i. (to meddle or interfere; to come between in another's private affairs)
etymology: From Old French entremedler, entre, between, + medler, to mix; to mix oneself between two things that are properly left alone.
biblical_def:
The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.

Solomon's proverb names a double privacy that belongs to every human heart: its bitterness is its own to know, and its joy is likewise its own to hold, neither fully transferable to an outsider however close that outsider may stand. A stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy does not describe a refusal but an incapacity, an outsider simply cannot insert himself into the full reality of another's private gladness any more than he can fully taste another's private grief. The proverb sits among Solomon's many observations on the limits of human community, not to discourage fellowship but to be honest about what fellowship can and cannot reach; even the closest friend, the dearest spouse, touches another's inmost heart only partially, by sympathy and report, never by direct possession. This is precisely why Scripture roots ultimate comfort and ultimate joy in the LORD rather than in human companionship alone, He only, who searcheth the heart, truly knows its bitterness, and He only can intermeddle, so to speak, with its joy from the inside, which no stranger, however well-meaning, ever fully can.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from MEDDLE: to interfere between; to involve oneself in what belongs properly to another.
webster_full: MEDDLE, v.i. To interpose or interfere officiously in others' affairs.
INTERMEDDLE, v.i. To come between; to meddle or interfere with another's private matter.
Proverbs 14: a stranger doth not intermeddle with another's joy, as he cannot share his bitterness.
Names the privacy of the heart, both its grief and its gladness.
Roots ultimate comfort in the LORD, who alone truly searches the heart.
scriptures: The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is the limit of human sympathy against any claim of total mutual transparency.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Intermeddle has simply fallen into disuse, its sense largely absorbed into the plainer meddle.

The proverb's honesty is worth recovering against any ideal of community, therapeutic or romantic, that promises total mutual access to another's inner life. Solomon does not counsel isolation, but he refuses to pretend that fellowship can do what only the LORD, who searcheth the heart, actually can. A friendship that demands to fully intermeddle with another's private joy or grief is asking of man what Scripture reserves for God.

etymology: From king, Old English cyning, + the adjectival -ly; naming whatever belongs properly to, or is fit for, royal rule.
biblical_def:
But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him.

Daniel is recounting Nebuchadnezzar's own testimony to Belshazzar's court, a public confession written into the historical record of how the greatest king of his age had been humbled. Kingly throne names the full height of Nebuchadnezzar's actual power, builder of Babylon, conqueror of nations, a throne that was genuinely, not merely nominally, royal. The deposing came not from a rival king but from the LORD Himself, and for one specific cause named plainly, his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, as though sovereignty this real could be credited to the sovereign's own greatness rather than received from above. Daniel includes this testimony immediately before Belshazzar's own feast, where the same pride, unhumbled by his grandfather's example, leads to the writing on the wall and the kingdom's loss that very night. The pairing is deliberate: kingly glory, wherever it is found, belongs to the LORD's loan rather than a man's own achievement, and the Book of Daniel insists twice in successive chapters that a throne forgetting this does not keep what it was given.

webster_full: KING, n. The sovereign of a nation; a monarch.

His own testimony is read before Belshazzar's court, as a warning unheeded.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Kingly survives chiefly as a literary flourish today, its theological weight as a word about sovereignty received from God having mostly faded.

The history behind it still convicts any position of real power, political, corporate, or personal, that begins to credit itself for what it was given. Nebuchadnezzar's own testimony, read aloud before Belshazzar, was meant as a warning his grandson ignored that very night. Kingly glory, Daniel insists twice over, is held at the LORD's pleasure, and a heart lifted up in pride does not keep what it forgets it received.

pos: v.t. (to pour out or spend profusely; to squander on an unworthy object)
etymology: From Old French lavasse, a deluge of rain, from laver, to wash; a word for abundance poured out without restraint, applied in the KJV to abundance misdirected.
biblical_def:
They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship.

Isaiah's indictment of idol-making is precise about sequence and cost: real gold, carefully weighed silver, a hired craftsman's genuine skill, all poured out, lavished, on an object that the lavishing itself produces, a god made rather than found. The verb exposes the absurdity at the center of every idolatry, resources are freely squandered to manufacture the very thing then bowed before as though it had manufactured them. Isaiah's larger argument throughout this section contrasts such a god, carried because it cannot carry itself, with the LORD, who bears His people even to old age, I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you. Lavish names the idolater's investment, real wealth, real labor, genuinely spent, which makes the irony sharper rather than softer: the problem with idolatry is never that too little was given to it, but that anything at all was given to a god of one's own making rather than received from the God who made the giver.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LAVISH: to expend or pour out with profusion; to squander, especially upon an unworthy object.
webster_full: LAVISH, a. Expending or bestowing without stint; profuse.
LAVISH, v.t. To expend with profusion; to squander.
Isaiah 46: idolaters lavish gold and silver on a god of their own making.
Contrasted with the LORD, who carries His people rather than being carried.
Exposes idolatry's irony: real wealth spent to manufacture a false object of worship.
scriptures: Isa 46:6
They lavish gold out of the bag, and weigh silver in the balance, and hire a goldsmith; and he maketh it a god: they fall down, yea, they worship.
corruption_summary: Consumer culture lavishes resources on self-made objects of devotion with the same irony Isaiah names, only the gold is now time, attention, and money spent on image and comfort.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern materialism lavishes real resources, income, attention, labor, on objects it then effectively worships, status, image, comfort, exactly as Isaiah's idolaters hired a goldsmith to build what they would then fall down before.

Isaiah's contrast remains the cure: a god assembled from one's own lavished wealth must be carried, borne, is a burden to the weary beast, while the LORD who made His people carries them instead. Whatever a person lavishes their resources upon to produce a sense of security or worth has become, by Isaiah's own definition, a candidate for exactly this idolatry, however unreligious it looks.

pos: adv. (in a base, lustful, or wicked manner; lasciviously)
etymology: From lewd, Old English laewede, originally lay, unlearned, which narrowed over centuries to base, vile, and then specifically to sexually immoral.
biblical_def:
And one hath committed abomination with his neighbour's wife; and another hath lewdly defiled his daughter in law; and another in thee hath humbled his sister, his father's daughter.

Ezekiel's catalogue of Jerusalem's sins piles indictment on indictment, and lewdly here marks the specific, deliberate quality of one man's incest with his daughter-in-law, defilement entered into knowingly and shamelessly rather than committed in ignorance. The list functions as Ezekiel's answer to a besieged city's self-image: Jerusalem imagined itself as the LORD's own, yet in thee men have done what even pagan nations would recognize as unnatural, adultery, incest, violence, usury, oppression of the stranger, fatherless, and widow. Lewdly intensifies defiled into something beyond mere transgression, a willful plunge into exactly the kind of sexual corruption the law had named by name as detestable; the word does not describe weakness overcome but wickedness pursued. The chapter's governing metaphor, a besieged and melting city, a dross to be refined in the furnace of the LORD's fury, treats this moral catalogue as the actual cause of the coming siege, not an incidental footnote to it; Jerusalem's walls fall because what happened inside them had already fallen first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from LEWD: in a lewd manner; lasciviously; with base, lustful wickedness.
webster_full: LEWD, a. Given to the unlawful indulgence of lust; debauched; lustful.
LEWDLY, adv. In a lewd manner; lasciviously; wickedly.
Ezekiel 22: one man hath lewdly defiled his daughter in law, among a catalogue of Jerusalem's sins.

corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is Ezekiel's refusal to separate a nation's sexual corruption from its coming judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Lewdly has simply narrowed in modern speech to a mild word for crudeness, far short of the deliberate wickedness Ezekiel names.

The chapter behind it still resists any theology that treats a culture's private sexual sin as spiritually separable from its public judgment. Ezekiel does not list this catalogue as background color to the siege of Jerusalem; he names it as cause. A people that has, like Jerusalem, learned to call the LORD's own name while tolerating exactly what His law named detestable should not expect the two to remain unconnected for long.
roots_summary: From Old English laewede, lay or unlearned, lewd narrowed over centuries to base and then specifically to lustful; Ezekiel applies the adverb to deliberate, knowing defilement.
